focus: Broad (all career and work psychology topics)

studies.title: A short nudge changed how managers responded to a downturn — and the effect grew over three months
studies.paper_title: Counteracting threat bias: A longitudinal field experiment testing two interventions that expand managerial attention to opportunities under economic threat.
studies.the_study: In a five-wave field experiment run during the COVID-19 economic downturn, 414 managers were randomly assigned to one of two brief 'construal-shaping' interventions — one highlighting opportunities, one highlighting both opportunities and threats — or to a control group. Opportunity-related and threat-related voice was rated by higher-level managers blind to condition. Among untreated managers, when perceived threat rose they shifted toward a prevention focus and spoke up less about opportunities; both interventions broke that link and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice, with effects that grew over three months. The balanced version additionally raised prevention focus and threat-related voice, suggesting vigilance and opportunity-seeking are not a zero-sum trade-off.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests organizations do not have to split 'defensive' and 'growth' roles across different people during a crisis — the same managers can be helped to attend to both, with a low-cost intervention rather than restructuring.
studies.story_angle_primary: For leaders planning through a downturn: the study is a rare randomized field test showing that how a crisis is framed to managers, not how severe they judge it to be, shapes whether they still surface growth ideas. Worth testing in your own leadership communications — do your town halls and dashboards cue only loss prevention?
studies.story_angle_secondary: A counterintuitive window into how fear works at work: the intervention did not make managers feel safer or perceive less threat, it changed what they did with the threat they already felt — a reminder that mindset interventions can reroute a reaction without denying the reality behind it.
studies.caveats: Single-author study; conducted during a specific and unusual macro shock (COVID-19), which may limit generalization to ordinary downturns; three-month horizon; voice outcomes rated by supervisors rather than measured as business results.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, N (414), five waves, blind supervisor-rated voice and the three-month growth all match. Two small wording slips: the abstract reports lower promotion focus (not a shift toward prevention focus) and says interventions "weakened" rather than broke the threat–voice association.

studies.title: Overqualified and over 50: feeling underused pushes older workers to mentor, not to disengage
studies.paper_title: Passing on Talent: A Generativity Perspective on the Effects of Perceived Overqualification Among Older Employees
studies.the_study: Two field studies tested whether perceived overqualification plays out differently for older employees: a three-wave survey of 261 older workers, and a three-wave dyadic study of 274 employee–supervisor pairs across age groups. Older employees who felt overqualified reported a stronger generativity motive — the desire to guide and be needed by the next generation — which in turn predicted finding prosocial meaning in work and engaging in more helping behavior. HR practices tailored to mature-age workers strengthened that pathway.
studies.why_it_matters: Overqualification is usually framed as a liability linked to boredom, cynicism and turnover; this suggests that for older staff it can be channeled into mentoring and knowledge transfer if the organization gives it an outlet.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you manage experienced staff whose jobs no longer stretch them, the actionable test is whether formal mentoring, knowledge-transfer or training roles convert surplus capability into contribution instead of disengagement — and whether your 'mature-age' HR offerings exist at all.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone in the later stretch of a career who feels their skills exceed the job: the study points to a meaningful second answer besides leaving — being useful to the people coming up behind you.
studies.caveats: Self-report predictors and mediators; Study 1 is single-source across waves (common-method concerns); correlational despite the time lags, so causation is not established; moderate sample sizes; context and country not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Two three-wave field studies, N = 261 and N = 274 dyads, the generativity pathway and the mature-age HR practices moderator are all reported as in the abstract; caveats appropriately flag self-report, common method and the correlational design.

studies.title: Women get asked for advice as often as men — but only if they're seen as highly prosocial
studies.paper_title: Closing the Gap, Carrying the Burden: How Gender and Prosocial Motivation Shape Workplace Recognition
studies.the_study: A time-lagged, multi-source field study (n=275) plus two preregistered-style online experiments (n=247 and n=248) examined who becomes a go-to advice source at work. Women occupied less central positions in advice networks than men, but that gap closed among women high in prosocial motivation. Advice centrality then mediated effects on leadership emergence and supervisor performance ratings, meaning the network position translated into real recognition.
studies.why_it_matters: It identifies a concrete mechanism behind unequal recognition — who colleagues turn to for advice — and shows that the route to parity for women may carry an extra, unreciprocated helping burden.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers can audit who actually gets consulted on their team and whether visibility is being purchased by women through extra helping that men don't have to perform. Formal recognition of expertise, rather than leaving it to informal advice-seeking, is the testable fix.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A sharp illustration of the 'office housework' bind: being generous does get women noticed, but the fact that it is required of them and not of men is itself the inequality.
studies.caveats: The field study is correlational with modest N and the setting/country is unspecified; the two experiments used online participants and hypothetical judgments rather than real colleagues; the 'burden' asymmetry is theorized from the pattern, not directly measured as cost to women.
studies.verdict_notes: Samples (275; 247; 248) and the mediation model match. Small issues: the abstract does not describe the experiments as preregistered, does not specify who provided performance ratings, and measures prosocial motivation rather than how prosocial a woman is perceived to be.

studies.title: Status comes first: being liked and respected builds power faster than power builds respect
studies.paper_title: The Asymmetric Nature of Social Hierarchies: Unpacking the Dynamic Relationship Between Power and Status
studies.the_study: Across two studies of real project teams, researchers used bivariate dual change score models — a dynamic method borrowed from developmental psychology — to track how power and status influenced each other over time, plus three follow-up experiments. The two did reinforce each other, but asymmetrically: status predicted later gains in power more strongly than power predicted later gains in status. The experiments showed perceived communality (warmth, concern for others) explained the asymmetry, and the pattern held whether power was formal or based on informal control of resources.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the assumption that getting the title or budget authority will eventually earn you standing — the evidence runs more strongly the other way.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone promoted into authority: control of resources does not reliably convert into being respected, but being seen as competent and communal does convert into real control. Watch for newly promoted managers who lean on positional power and lose influence.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A useful corrective to career advice built around chasing titles: the long game of being the person people respect appears to generate more leverage than the short game of acquiring formal clout.
studies.caveats: Field data come from project teams (composition and country unspecified), with the causal mechanism tested only in separate experiments; dynamic modeling of observational data still cannot fully rule out confounds; experiment participants likely online or student samples judging scenarios.
studies.verdict_notes: Two project-team studies with bivariate dual change score models, three additional experiments, the communality mechanism and the formal/informal power robustness check are all reported faithfully. One story-angle addition ("competent") is not in the abstract.

studies.title: Moderately good-looking male founders fare best; for women, looks barely move the needle
studies.paper_title: Appearance-Based Legitimate Distinctiveness: Founder Attractiveness, Gender, and Venture Evaluations
studies.the_study: Researchers tested competing 'beauty premium' and 'beauty-is-beastly' predictions by proposing that founder appearance is judged through two opposing channels — perceived legitimacy and perceived distinctiveness. In a field study of 359 founders, male founders received the best venture evaluations when moderately attractive, while attractiveness showed no significant effect for female founders. A preregistered experiment with 771 participants using AI-manipulated attractiveness did not reproduce the gendered field pattern but did support the two-mediator mechanism.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests investor and evaluator judgments of startups are partly driven by whether a founder looks like the prototype of an entrepreneur — a bias founders can't control and evaluators rarely acknowledge.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone screening pitches or candidates: the finding is a prompt to check whether appearance-driven impressions of 'legitimacy' are quietly riding along in evaluation scores, and whether structured rubrics could strip them out.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A glimpse at how superficial first impressions shape who gets backed — and a reminder that the advantage, where it exists, is for looking plausibly typical, not for looking exceptional.
studies.caveats: The field study is correlational with a modest sample and attractiveness ratings of founders; the preregistered experiment failed to replicate the central gendered pattern, which weakens confidence in it; experiment used AI-manipulated images and hypothetical venture evaluations rather than real investment decisions; context/country not specified.
studies.verdict_notes: Field study (359 founders), preregistered experiment (771 participants, AI-manipulated attractiveness), the inverted-U for men, the null for women and the non-replication of the gendered pattern alongside support for the two mediators are all accurately represented, and the caveats flag the failed replication.

studies.title: The UK's "bamboo ceiling" is real — but only for some Asian groups, and mostly for men
studies.paper_title: The Bamboo Ceiling in the UK: Ethnicity–Gender Intersectionality, Risk Tolerance, and Leadership Attainment
studies.the_study: Researchers combined two datasets: a 14-year census of CEOs and CFOs at FTSE-listed companies (2011–2024), and the UK Biobank cohort (N=322,734). Ethnic Chinese executives were virtually absent from the FTSE top jobs, while ethnic Indians were represented at rates statistically indistinguishable from White Britons. In the Biobank data, the leadership gap for ethnic Chinese was driven by men — Chinese men were less likely than Indian or White men to hold leadership roles, partly explained by lower measured risk tolerance (results held using both survey and polygenic risk-tolerance measures) — while Chinese, Indian and White women were all equally disadvantaged relative to men of their own group.
studies.why_it_matters: Treating "Asian" as one category in diversity reporting hides a near-total absence of one subgroup from the top of British business, and shows that the barriers differ sharply by gender.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your organization reports ethnicity data in broad bands, disaggregate it: subgroup-level analysis may reveal leadership gaps that aggregate numbers conceal. Also worth questioning whether promotion criteria implicitly reward displays of risk appetite rather than results.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The "model minority" label is a statistical illusion built from averages — and it can leave the people it supposedly flatters invisible in the rooms where decisions get made.
studies.caveats: Observational and correlational; risk tolerance is a partial mediator, not a demonstrated cause, and polygenic measures of a trait like risk tolerance are contested. UK Biobank participants are not a representative sample of the UK population (volunteer bias, older skew). Single-country.
studies.verdict_notes: FTSE 2011–2024 census, UK Biobank N=322,734, the Chinese/Indian contrast, the gender moderation and the robustness across survey and polygenic risk-tolerance measures all match. One small inference beyond the abstract on the direction of the risk-tolerance difference.

studies.title: Founders with dark-triad traits pick co-founders very differently — and equity is their trigger
studies.paper_title: Co-founder selection from a marriage market perspective: How the dark triad shapes judgments of interpersonal attraction, resources, and equity demand
studies.the_study: A conjoint experiment put 206 practicing entrepreneurs through 3,296 simulated co-founder selection decisions, varying candidates' interpersonal appeal, resource contributions and equity demands. Overall, founders were drawn to likable candidates and to those bringing resources, and were put off by high equity demands. But lead founders scoring higher on the dark triad (narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy) largely discounted interpersonal attraction and reacted far more strongly to equity dilution — a shift from joint value creation toward personal payoff.
studies.why_it_matters: Co-founder choice shapes a venture's survival, and this suggests the personality of the person doing the choosing systematically bends what "a good partner" means.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone being recruited into a founding team: how a lead founder reacts to your equity ask may be a cheap diagnostic of how they will handle future splits of value. For investors and accelerators, founder personality is a lens on team composition, not just on the individual.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The paper borrows from marriage-market theory — and finds the same thing dating research does: what someone says they want in a partner depends a lot on who they are.
studies.caveats: A conjoint experiment with hypothetical candidate profiles, not real co-founder decisions; dark triad self-reported in the same session as the choices; modest sample of 206 entrepreneurs and unspecified national context.
studies.verdict_notes: Conjoint experiment, 206 entrepreneurs, 3,296 decisions, the main effects of interpersonal attraction, resources and equity demand, and the dark-triad shift toward personal utility all match the abstract; the hypothetical-profile caveat is appropriately stated.

studies.title: Why bank AI projects stall: it's not the black box, it's the clash over what counts as proof
studies.paper_title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
studies.the_study: An 18-month inductive field study inside three large Indian banks tracked how data scientists and domain experts fought over predictive AI models. The conflict was epistemic — the two groups disagreed over how knowledge should be produced and evaluated — rather than a simple turf war, and domain experts held veto power over deployment. Direct attempts to win the argument on one side's terms failed; what eventually worked were four "bridging" practices that embedded model predictions inside the documents, routines and boundary objects domain experts already used.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes AI adoption failure as a knowledge-standards problem, suggesting that translating model output into the formats experts already trust beats explaining the algorithm better.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your analytics team's models keep dying before deployment, stop investing only in explainability dashboards and start asking which existing reports, checklists and review meetings the predictions could be folded into. Note also who actually holds the veto — often expertise-based power, not formal authority.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A window into what "AI is coming for your job" looks like day to day: experienced staff rarely get overruled by a model — they decide whether anyone ever sees it.
studies.caveats: Qualitative study of three banks in one country and one sector; findings are interpretive and not statistically generalizable; no measure of whether the bridging practices improved business outcomes.
studies.verdict_notes: 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, the epistemic-versus-jurisdictional distinction, domain experts' deployment power, the failure of assimilative practices and the four bridging practices are all reported faithfully, with appropriate qualitative caveats.

studies.title: The "identity pause": what perimenopausal workers did instead of pushing through
studies.paper_title: The Power of Identity Pause: Perimenopause and the Embodiment Process
studies.the_study: An inductive qualitative study of women going through perimenopause examined how bodily change collided with the professional identities they believed they should be enacting. Rather than the remedial identity work or body work documented in earlier research, the key mechanism was an "identity pause" — deliberately stepping back from striving to perform an idealized self — which created room for "somatic attunement," the capacity to listen to and work with a changing body.
studies.why_it_matters: Perimenopause affects most women, often at the peak career stage, and this suggests the useful organizational response is permission to ease off temporarily rather than accommodations aimed at restoring full performance of the old self.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers reviewing mid-career women who suddenly seem less driven should consider whether what's needed is a sanctioned period of reduced identity pressure — not a performance conversation. Also a prompt to check whether your workplace treats menopause as a health footnote or a career-stage reality.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A counterintuitive lesson that extends beyond menopause: when your body changes — illness, injury, aging, new parenthood — trying harder to be the old version of yourself may be exactly what blocks the adjustment.
studies.caveats: Qualitative, inductive theory-building; sample size and composition not specified in the abstract; no outcome data on careers or performance; findings describe mechanisms, not prevalence or effectiveness.
studies.verdict_notes: The identity pause and somatic attunement mechanisms and the contrast with remedial identity/body work match the abstract. "Why it matters" adds a career-stage claim and a prescriptive organizational response that the abstract does not support.

studies.title: Side-hustle founders aren't on a runway to full-time — for many, hybrid is the destination
studies.paper_title: Transitional Path or Optimal State? Hybrid Entrepreneurship and the Decisions to Enter and Exit Entrepreneurship
studies.the_study: Using large-scale US data, researchers tested two rival accounts of hybrid entrepreneurship (running a venture while holding a job): is it a transitional stage toward full-time founding, or a stable optimal arrangement in its own right? By examining how hybrid status changed the effect of switching costs on both entry into full-time entrepreneurship and exit from entrepreneurship altogether, they found patterns more consistent with the "state" perspective — hybrid entrepreneurs as a group are not simply en route to quitting their jobs.
studies.why_it_matters: Policies, accelerator programs and investor expectations built on the assumption that side ventures should "graduate" to full-time may be misreading what most hybrid founders actually want.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you manage people with side businesses, the common fear that they are one funding round from resigning is probably overstated — and the more useful question is how to coexist with a durable arrangement. For would-be founders, keeping the job may be a strategy rather than a lack of nerve.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The quit-your-job founding myth takes another hit: for a lot of people the side business is the business, not the audition for one.
studies.caveats: Archival observational data from a single country (US); the abstract gives no sample size, data source or effect magnitudes; inferences about motive are drawn from behavioral patterns rather than measured intentions.
studies.verdict_notes: The transition-versus-state framing, the switching-cost test on entry and exit, the large-scale U.S. data and the conclusion favouring the state perspective all match; the caveats correctly note the absence of sample details and that motives are inferred from behaviour.

studies.title: When a supportive boss makes perfectionists work themselves into the ground
studies.paper_title: The trap of appearing perfect: When servant leaders accidentally intensify follower over-commitment and workaholism
studies.the_study: Researchers tested whether employees driven to appear flawless — a trait called perfectionistic self-presentation — end up overworking, and whether a caring leader makes it better or worse. Across three time-lagged field studies with working adults (two in China, one in the United Kingdom), employees high in perfectionistic self-presentation reported higher workaholism, and the path ran through over-commitment to their leader. Crucially, the effect was strongest under servant leadership — the style built on serving, developing and putting followers first.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that the leadership styles organizations promote as humane can quietly intensify overwork in the employees most prone to it, because a leader who invests in you becomes an audience you feel you must never disappoint.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers who pride themselves on supporting their people should watch for the direct report who never visibly struggles: these field data suggest your generosity may be read as an obligation to look perfect. Test whether explicitly normalizing visible mistakes, capping after-hours responsiveness and separating "support" from "evaluation" changes behavior on your own team.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A great boss is not automatically good for your health. If you find yourself working late mainly so a leader who has been kind to you is never let down, the loyalty you feel may be doing the same damage as a demanding manager would.
studies.caveats: Time-lagged surveys rather than experiments, so causality remains inferential; key variables including workaholism are self-reported by the same employees who rated their leaders, raising common-method concerns; samples drawn from two countries only and effects concern perceptions of leadership rather than observed leader behavior.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, country split (two China, one UK), mediator (overcommitment to leader) and the servant-leadership amplification are all reported correctly; caveats flag common-method and inferential causality.

studies.title: For veterans going back to school, hope only pays off if it turns into action
studies.paper_title: Testing the Career Construction Model of Adaptation With Student Veterans
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 276 US student veterans and used structural equation modeling to test a career-adaptation pathway: personal resources, then adapting behaviors, then life outcomes. Both "hope agency thinking" (the belief you can pursue your goals) and proactive personality were linked to life satisfaction only indirectly — through occupational engagement, meaning concrete activities like exploring careers, talking to people in target fields and testing options. Neither trait related to satisfaction on its own.
studies.why_it_matters: It points career counselors and employers working with transitioning service members toward structured exploration activity rather than motivation or mindset alone, since the behavior appears to be what links disposition to well-being.
studies.story_angle_primary: Employers and universities running veteran transition programs could test whether adding structured occupational exploration — informational interviews, job shadowing, trial projects — outperforms resilience and mindset workshops, which this study suggests do little unless they produce action.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone reinventing a career after a major life change, the pattern is a useful corrective: feeling hopeful and proactive did not track with a more satisfying life unless it showed up as actual exploratory behavior.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional self-report survey, so the causal ordering is assumed rather than demonstrated; single population (US student veterans) limits generalization; all measures from the same source at one time point.
studies.verdict_notes: N, sample and the two indirect pathways are correct; one sentence slightly overstates the absence of direct effects.

studies.title: Harassed by a customer, with no one watching: what protects gig workers
studies.paper_title: You are not alone: access to collective representation buffers the harmful impact of customer sexual harassment on gig workers
studies.the_study: Researchers ran two studies with US gig workers: a five-day diary study (99 workers, 373 daily observations) and a three-wave time-separated survey (N=377). On days after experiencing customer sexual harassment, workers reported higher psychological distress and a greater sense of threat to the self, and in turn cut corners on the work itself (production deviance) and behaved more rudely or hostilely toward customers (interpersonal deviance). Those harmful knock-on effects were significantly weaker among workers who had access to some form of collective representation, such as a union, worker association or organized peer body.
studies.why_it_matters: Gig platforms strip out the bystanders, HR channels and repeat relationships that normally constrain customer harassment, and the fallout shows up in the quality of the work itself — but simply having a collective body to turn to appears to blunt the damage.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers and platform operators who rely on contract and gig labor should ask what reporting route a harassed worker actually has; the study suggests that access to collective representation is not just a labor-relations issue but a performance and service-quality one.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone driving, delivering or doing freelance client-facing work, the finding puts numbers on a familiar experience: a single bad customer interaction spills into the rest of the day's work, and feeling that someone has your back materially changes how much it costs you.
studies.caveats: Self-report measures of distress and deviance in both studies raise common-method concerns; US gig workers only; 99 participants in the diary study; "access to collective representation" is measured, not randomly assigned, so workers with access may differ in other ways.
studies.verdict_notes: Samples, observation counts and the buffering finding are accurate; the two mediator pathways are merged and the examples of "collective representation" are not in the abstract.

studies.title: Money worries make employees angry — and the anger shows up in their work
studies.paper_title: The emotional tax of financial insecurity: a dual-study examination of anger’s role in work behaviour
studies.journal: European Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology
studies.the_study: Two multi-wave, time-lagged studies tested whether financial insecurity harms work behavior through anger. Study 1 followed 190 working university students in the US across three waves with multi-source ratings; Study 2 followed 189 full-time employees in Belgium across four waves of self-reports. In both, employees who felt their financial resources were inadequate or unstable reported more anger, and that anger predicted more counterproductive work behavior; evidence for an effect on task performance was weaker.
studies.why_it_matters: Financial stress is usually treated as a private matter, but these results suggest it leaks into the workplace as anger and rule-breaking rather than simply as reduced output — a different problem requiring a different response.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers seeing an uptick in friction, rule-bending or incivility might consider economic pressure as a driver, and weigh whether financial-wellness benefits, pay predictability or earned-wage access do more for behavior than another performance conversation.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The study names something many workers recognize: being broke or precarious does not just make you tired, it makes you short-tempered — and the target is often colleagues or the employer rather than the actual source of the stress.
studies.caveats: Study 1's sample is working students, not a full-time workforce; Study 2 is entirely self-report, so anger and counterproductive behavior come from the same source; time-lagged designs establish temporal order but not causation; samples just under 200 each; effects on task performance were weak.
studies.verdict_notes: Samples, waves and countries are exact; headline and body use causal verbs for what the abstract calls associations, and the weaker task-performance evidence is attributed to both studies.

studies.title: Why bold ideas die on the boss's desk: it depends on how creative the boss is
studies.paper_title: When and Why Do Leaders Endorse Radical Ideas? A Transactional Theory of Stress Perspective
studies.the_study: A three-wave field study of 167 leader–employee dyads, plus a scenario-based experiment with 300 leaders, examined why radical ideas get rejected. The more radical the idea, the more threatened leaders felt — and the less likely they were to endorse it — but only when the leader scored low on creative personality. Leaders high in creative personality appraised radical proposals as less threatening and were more likely to back them.
studies.why_it_matters: The usual advice tells employees how to pitch; this says the decisive variable may be who they are pitching to, and that organizations wanting radical innovation need to manage leaders' threat responses, not just employees' persuasion skills.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before championing a radical proposal, assess the decision-maker: with a leader who is not personally creative, framing matters less than reducing perceived threat — pilot scale, reversibility, shared ownership. Organizations should also ask whether idea-screening is being routed to people temperamentally disposed to feel endangered by novelty.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It reframes a common career frustration — your best idea got killed and you assumed it was politics or your own poor selling. The research suggests the idea may simply have landed on someone who experienced it as a personal risk.
studies.caveats: The replication study used hypothetical scenarios rather than real endorsement decisions; the field study is dyadic survey data across three waves, so causal claims are limited; 167 dyads is modest; creative personality is self-reported.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes, the three-wave dyadic design, the 300-leader scenario replication and the direction of the moderation (including the decreased-threat path for high-creative leaders) match the abstract.

studies.title: Can you train people to make work more playful? Only if they do the exercises
studies.paper_title: Boosting playful work design: a test of a micro and modular e-intervention
studies.the_study: Researchers built and tested two online interventions to cultivate "playful work design" — deliberately injecting fun and self-set challenge into ordinary tasks. Study 1 was a micro-intervention (74 people, 432 daily observations) and Study 2 a modular e-intervention (127 people, 549 weekly observations). Actively completing the exercises increased designing competition in both studies and designing fun in Study 2; merely being exposed to the material predicted nothing. Playful work design was in turn linked to creative performance, via informal learning in Study 1 and self-efficacy in Study 2.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests playfulness at work is a trainable skill rather than a personality trait, and offers a cheap, low-touch format — but only for employees who actually engage with the exercises.
studies.story_angle_primary: A realistic test for managers skeptical of wellness content: offer a short, modular online program and track completion, not attendance. The finding that passive exposure did nothing is a warning about every broadcast-only training rollout.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For individuals stuck in repetitive work, the research hints that turning tasks into self-set games or challenges is something you can deliberately practice — and that the easier half, competing with yourself, responds faster than the harder half, manufacturing fun.
studies.caveats: Small samples (74 and 127 participants) with self-selected engagement, so the people who completed exercises likely differ from those who did not; self-reported creative performance; no clear randomized control comparison described; short time horizon.
studies.verdict_notes: Both study Ns, observation counts, the fun/competition split across studies, the null for mere exposure and the informal-learning/self-efficacy mediators are all reported correctly.

studies.title: Not all career dithering is the same: five reasons people stall on big decisions
studies.paper_title: Career Decisional Procrastination Questionnaire: Construction and Initial Validation
studies.the_study: Researchers developed and validated a questionnaire distinguishing five reasons people delay career decisions: chasing short-term rewards, protecting self-worth, lacking psychological resources, thriving under pressure, and strategic timing. It was tested in two Hebrew-speaking Israeli samples (N=240; N=243) and one English-speaking US sample (N=322). The five-factor structure held up, and the measure predicted career distress and commitment better than existing one-dimensional procrastination scales — with short-term rewards, self-worth protection and depleted resources tied to distress and rumination, while pressure thriving and strategic timing showed more mixed, sometimes adaptive patterns.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the assumption that delaying a career decision is always a problem: waiting for better information or working best near a deadline looks different from avoiding a decision to protect your ego.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone coaching or managing people through internal moves, promotions or role changes, the actionable point is to diagnose the reason for the delay before pushing — the intervention for someone out of psychological resources is nothing like the one for someone deliberately holding out for timing.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Readers agonizing over a job change can use the taxonomy on themselves: is this strategic patience, or is it avoidance dressed up as patience? The study suggests self-worth protection and short-term distraction are the versions that predict real distress.
studies.caveats: Scale-development research: cross-sectional, self-report, with no behavioral outcomes or follow-up on actual career decisions; samples from two countries only; incremental validity gains over existing measures are not quantified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Factor names, three samples and incremental validity are correct; the framing is slightly more favorable to "strategic timing" than the abstract warrants.

studies.title: When the boss makes everything a moral issue, employees stop fixing problems
studies.paper_title: The moralization paradox at work: How Supervisor's moral framing depletes subordinates' self‐regulatory resources and suppresses proactive problem prevention
studies.journal: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology
studies.the_study: Researchers tested what happens when supervisors frame ordinary work in moral terms — duty, right and wrong, doing good — using two complementary studies: an experience sampling study tracking employees and their supervisors over repeated daily measurements, and a vignette-based laboratory experiment. Across both, supervisor "work moralization" left subordinates feeling ego-depleted, and depleted employees did less proactive problem prevention — the self-initiated work of spotting and heading off future disruptions. The effect was strongest for employees high in reflective moral attentiveness, the people who think most carefully about the ethics of what they do.
studies.why_it_matters: Moral framing is widely treated as a free motivational good — purpose-driven leadership, values talk, mission language — but this evidence suggests it carries a self-regulatory tax that quietly suppresses exactly the discretionary, forward-looking behavior managers say they want.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers who lean on moral language to motivate teams might audit how often they do it and whether the people most sensitive to ethical framing are also the ones who have stopped flagging problems early; the lab portion shows what can happen rather than guaranteeing it will in every workplace, so treat it as a prompt to watch for depletion, not proof that purpose talk backfires.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It offers a counterintuitive explanation for why conscientious, ethically engaged employees often burn out first: constantly weighing the moral stakes of routine work consumes mental energy that would otherwise go into noticing and preventing the next mess.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes and country are not reported in the abstract; Study 2 relies on hypothetical vignettes rather than real work decisions; the experience sampling study is observational and short-horizon, so causal claims rest largely on the lab experiment; self-reported depletion and proactivity measures raise common-method concerns.
studies.verdict_notes: Mechanism (ego depletion), outcome (proactive problem prevention), moderator (reflective moral attentiveness) and the two-study design match; the description of the experience sampling study adds detail the abstract does not contain.

studies.title: Office politics can fuel creativity — but only where the boss plays favorites on merit
studies.paper_title: Navigating power dynamics: the role of political skill in fostering employee creativity
studies.the_study: Using matched supervisor–subordinate data from 247 employees across 50 teams in a Sino-Japanese joint venture in Taiwan, researchers tested how employees' political skill — reading people, building influence, navigating power — relates to supervisor-rated creativity. Political skill predicted creativity entirely through the quality of the employee's relationship with their manager (leader–member exchange); the direct link disappeared once that relationship was accounted for. The boost was strongest in teams where managers varied relationship quality according to performance rather than arbitrarily.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes political skill as a route to the managerial access and resources that creative work requires, and suggests that unequal manager–employee relationships are not automatically corrosive — provided the inequality visibly tracks performance.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers who worry that differentiating between team members breeds resentment might instead examine whether the basis for that differentiation is transparent and performance-linked; and leaders betting on creativity training alone may be missing that ideas travel through relationships with the boss.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone who finds workplace politics distasteful, this is an uncomfortable finding: the skill of managing upward appears to be less about manipulation than about securing the kind of relationship in which your ideas get heard at all.
studies.caveats: Single organization in one country (a Sino-Japanese joint venture in Taiwan), cross-sectional design that cannot establish causation, political skill self-reported while creativity was supervisor-rated, and the mediation claim rests on correlational data from one point in time.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (247 employees, 50 teams, Sino-Japanese joint venture in Taiwan), full mediation via LMX and the performance-based differentiation moderator are reported accurately; the headline overstates the moderator as a necessary condition and uses causal phrasing.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- *Exposure is not development; action is.* The previous digest's "Leadership experience only builds a leader identity in people who remember the experience well" (W7213545411) and "Startup Experience Alone Doesn't Make Graduates More Employable" (W7208810968) are directly echoed by two new studies: "Can you train people to make work more playful? Only if they do the exercises" (W7214211158), where passive exposure to the material predicted nothing, and "For veterans going back to school, hope only pays off if it turns into action" (W7213930347), where hope and proactive personality mattered only through actual occupational exploration. Three runs' worth of evidence now point the same way.
- *Economic pressure reshapes behavior, not just mood.* "Job insecurity doesn't just stress people out — it makes them hide and scroll" (W7204954329) is extended by "Money worries make employees angry — and the anger shows up in their work" (W7215113460), which locates the damage in counterproductive behavior rather than reduced output, and by "A short nudge changed how managers responded to a downturn" (W7202103093), which again uses the promotion/prevention regulatory-focus machinery that drove the insecurity findings.
- *Evaluation by prototype keeps producing exclusion with no obvious villain.* "Standard personality tests may quietly screen out autistic job candidates" (W7207655302) and "Transgender and Non-Binary Workers Hit Barriers at Every Stage of the Employee Lifecycle" (W7211865783) are joined by "Moderately good-looking male founders fare best" (W7214669005), where evaluations track looking like a plausible founder, and "The UK's 'bamboo ceiling' is real" (W7220681324), where aggregate ethnicity reporting conceals a near-total absence at the top.

**Advances**
- *From the cost of rejecting ideas to the cause of it.* The previous digest's "Reject a good idea and people stop trusting you" (W7159739744) showed what rejection costs the decision-maker; the new "Why bold ideas die on the boss's desk" (W7214467692) supplies the upstream mechanism — radical ideas feel threatening, but only to leaders low in creative personality. Read together these are the two halves of one story about idea gatekeeping.
- *Disaggregation as method.* The person-centered turn flagged last run (bullying profiles W7207619744; first-generation support profiles W7212183752) advances into new territory: "Not all career dithering is the same" (W7214312495) splits a single procrastination score into five distinct motives with opposite correlates, and W7220681324 splits "Asian" into subgroups with opposite leadership outcomes.
- *Leadership effects keep depending on the follower.* "An inspiring vision only works on employees who already love the job" (W7204870087) is advanced by "When the boss makes everything a moral issue" (W7220998881), where the depletion effect is strongest in the most morally attentive employees, and "When a supportive boss makes perfectionists work themselves into the ground" (W7219177765), where servant leadership hurts precisely the employees most anxious to look flawless.

**Counterpoints**
- *Underload is not uniformly corrosive.* "When work gets boring, the damage shows up the same week" (W7204556045) treated underuse as a live risk; "Overqualified and over 50" (W7213969383) finds that among older workers, feeling underused can route into generativity, mentoring and prosocial meaning if the organization supplies an outlet. Age and available outlets, not underuse itself, appear to decide which way it breaks.
- *Warm leadership is not a free good.* Last run's leadership items framed the problem as credibility (W7204870087, W7207697928); this run's W7219177765 and W7220998881 argue the humane styles organizations actively promote carry their own costs.

**New themes**
- *AI arrives in the digest as an organizational-politics story.* "Why bank AI projects stall" (W7221037317) is the first AI-deployment study in this run of digests, and it reframes adoption failure as a fight over what counts as proof, with domain experts holding the veto — nothing in the previous digest covered this ground.
- *Entrepreneurship widens from capital allocation to founder psychology.* The previous digest's entrepreneurship coverage was investor behavior (W7211933722); this batch adds founder-side studies: co-founder choice bent by dark-triad traits (W7220450586) and hybrid entrepreneurship as a destination rather than a runway (W7214931138).
- *Embodiment and life stage enter the frame.* "The 'identity pause'" (W7220928682) on perimenopause has no antecedent in the previous digest and opens a career-stage thread distinct from the earlier generational-meaning work (W7213869505).
- *Gig labor and collective representation.* "Harassed by a customer, with no one watching" (W7218644956) introduces platform work and worker associations, absent last run.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch converge on the same uncomfortable finding — the org chart is not where influence lives. Status predicts later gains in power more strongly than power predicts status, with perceived warmth doing the work ("Status comes first," W7214338919); advice-network centrality, not title, is what converts into leadership emergence and performance ratings, and women reach it only by being seen as highly prosocial ("Women get asked for advice as often as men," W7214315853); political skill boosts rated creativity entirely through the relationship with the boss, with no direct effect left over ("Office politics can fuel creativity," W7212394179); and inside three large banks, the people who decided whether AI models ever got deployed were domain experts with expertise-based veto power, not the executives who commissioned them ("Why bank AI projects stall," W7221037317).

**Why pitch this now:** Companies are flattening hierarchies, thinning middle management and pushing AI tools down from the top on the assumption that formal mandate equals adoption — while this evidence says the decisive gatekeeping is informal, relational and largely invisible to the people holding the titles.

**Angle:** A feature on the shadow org chart — how influence actually accumulates at work, why newly promoted managers and top-down technology rollouts so often find their authority is inert, and who pays an extra toll (women, in advice networks) to get standing that others are granted. Fits a business and management readership making promotion and AI-deployment decisions, with a strong secondary pull for general readers who have watched a title fail to translate into being listened to.

**Potential headlines:**
- The People Who Actually Decide Things Are Not on the Org Chart
- Your Promotion Came With Authority. It Did Not Come With Influence.
- When Nobody Asks for Your Advice, Your Title Won't Save You

**Potential outlets:**
- **Harvard Business Review** — its core readership is newly promoted leaders and executives running AI rollouts, exactly the people whose formal power the evidence says is not converting.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — the bank AI study's expertise-based veto and "bridging practices" are precisely its analytics-adoption and governance beat.
- **Fast Company** — flattening and middle-manager cuts are a live beat there, and the "status before power" reversal is a sharp, contrarian read on what a promotion actually buys.
- **Fortune** — its leadership coverage can carry the gendered twist, where women reach the same network position only by paying a prosocial tax men are not asked for.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **A short nudge changed how managers responded to a downturn (Work ID W7202103093):** A rare randomized field test showing that crisis framing — not perceived severity — determines whether managers still surface growth ideas, and the effect grew over three months, for a manager-audience leadership column or a workplace news brief.
- **Overqualified and over 50 (Work ID W7213969383):** Overqualification is usually a turnover red flag, but for older workers it can convert into mentoring and knowledge transfer if there is an outlet — a direct challenge to how firms handle experienced staff in plateaued roles, for an HR explainer or a later-career advice column.
- **Women get asked for advice as often as men — but only if they're seen as highly prosocial (Work ID W7214315853):** Advice-seeking is the hidden mechanism behind unequal recognition, and parity for women appears to be purchased with extra helping, for a work-psychology explainer in a general-interest or women's/lifestyle outlet, with a manager-facing "audit who gets consulted" sidebar.
- **Status comes first (Work ID W7214338919):** Being respected converts into real control more reliably than control converts into respect — a corrective for title-chasing career advice and for newly promoted managers leaning on positional power, for a manager-audience column.
- **Moderately good-looking male founders fare best (Work ID W7214669005):** Appearance shapes venture evaluations through perceived legitimacy, and the advantage is for looking typical rather than exceptional — handle the failed experimental replication honestly, for an entrepreneurship or VC-focused piece.
- **The UK's "bamboo ceiling" is real (Work ID W7220681324):** Broad-band ethnicity reporting hides a near-total absence of ethnic Chinese executives from FTSE top jobs while ethnic Indian representation matches White Britons — a disaggregate-your-data story with a sharp "model minority is an average" line, for a DEI/HR explainer or a business-news feature.
- **Founders with dark-triad traits pick co-founders very differently (Work ID W7220450586):** How a lead founder reacts to your equity ask is a cheap diagnostic of how they will split value later, for a startup-careers piece or an accelerator/investor-audience column.
- **Why bank AI projects stall (Work ID W7221037317):** Model adoption fails over whose standards of proof count, not over explainability — the fix is folding predictions into the reports and routines experts already trust, for an AI-at-work or analytics-leadership explainer.
- **The "identity pause" (Work ID W7220928682):** Stepping back from performing an idealized professional self, rather than accommodations aimed at restoring the old self, is what the women in this study found workable — with a read-across to illness, injury and new parenthood, for a women's/lifestyle outlet or a general-interest work-psychology piece.
- **Side-hustle founders aren't on a runway to full-time (Work ID W7214931138):** Hybrid entrepreneurship looks like a stable destination, not an audition — which undercuts accelerator, policy and investor assumptions and defuses managers' fear that side-hustlers are about to resign, for a small-business or careers column.
- **When a supportive boss makes perfectionists work themselves into the ground (Work ID W7219177765):** Servant leadership intensifies workaholism in employees driven to appear flawless, because a generous leader becomes an audience you can never disappoint, for a manager-audience column and a general-interest piece on why a great boss isn't automatically good for you.
- **For veterans going back to school, hope only pays off if it turns into action (Work ID W7213930347):** Mindset and resilience workshops track with nothing unless they produce concrete exploration behavior — a testable design point for veteran and career-transition programs, for a career-advice column or an L&D/HR explainer.
- **Harassed by a customer, with no one watching (Work ID W7218644956):** Gig platforms strip out the bystanders and reporting routes that constrain customer harassment, and access to a union or worker association measurably blunts the spillover into work quality, for a labor/workplace news feature or a gig-economy explainer.
- **Money worries make employees angry (Work ID W7215113460):** Financial insecurity leaks into work as anger and rule-breaking rather than lower output, which points at pay predictability and financial-wellness benefits instead of performance conversations, for a benefits/HR explainer or a cost-of-living work story in a general-interest outlet.
- **Why bold ideas die on the boss's desk (Work ID W7214467692):** The decisive variable in whether a radical idea survives is the creative personality of the person you pitch to, not your pitch — reframe a familiar career frustration and give readers threat-reduction tactics, for a career-advice column or an innovation-management piece.
- **Can you train people to make work more playful? (Work ID W7214211158):** Completing the exercises worked; exposure to the material did nothing — a warning about every broadcast-only training rollout, plus a self-help angle on turning repetitive tasks into self-set challenges, for a manager-audience L&D column or a lifestyle work piece.
- **Not all career dithering is the same (Work ID W7214312495):** A five-way taxonomy separating strategic patience and deadline-thriving from self-worth protection and depleted resources, with only the latter predicting distress — ideal as a self-diagnostic, for a career-advice column in a general-interest or women's/lifestyle outlet.
- **When the boss makes everything a moral issue (Work ID W7220998881):** Purpose and values talk carries a self-regulatory tax that suppresses exactly the proactive problem-prevention managers want, and hits the most ethically attentive employees hardest — flag the vignette-based limits, for a leadership/internal-communications column.
- **Office politics can fuel creativity (Work ID W7212394179):** Political skill works entirely through the boss relationship, and visibly performance-linked favoritism beats arbitrary favoritism — an uncomfortable finding for anyone who treats managing upward as beneath them, for a career-advice column or a manager-audience piece on differentiation.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Career Psychology Digest — Broad (all career and work psychology topics) — 2026-11-11
**Checked:** 2026-11-11 | **Studies reviewed:** 19
**Primary audience:** working professionals and managers | **Secondary audience:** general readers

---

### Study 1: A short nudge changed how managers responded to a downturn — and the effect grew over three months
**Work ID:** W7202103093 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Direction of the baseline effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Among untreated managers, when perceived threat rose they shifted toward a prevention focus and spoke up less about opportunities"
- **Abstract says:** "Among unexposed managers, within-person increases in perceived threat were associated with lower promotion focus and opportunity-related voice, the threat-bias pattern."
- **Problem:** The abstract documents a drop in promotion focus, not a rise in prevention focus; under regulatory focus theory these are independent systems, which is the paper's core claim.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rewrite as: "when perceived threat rose, their promotion focus fell and they spoke up less about opportunities"."

**Issue B. "Broke that link" overstates** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "both interventions broke that link and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice"
- **Abstract says:** "Both interventions weakened that association and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice relative to control"
- **Problem:** "Broke" implies the association was eliminated; the abstract says it was weakened.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "weakened that link"."

### Study 2: Overqualified and over 50: feeling underused pushes older workers to mentor, not to disengage
**Work ID:** W7213969383 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Women get asked for advice as often as men — but only if they're seen as highly prosocial
**Work ID:** W7214315853 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Preregistration not stated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "two preregistered-style online experiments (n=247 and n=248)"
- **Abstract says:** "Two online experiments (Study 2a, n = 247; Study 2b, n = 248) provide converging causal evidence for these effects."
- **Problem:** The abstract makes no claim about preregistration; "preregistered-style" is an invented methodological descriptor that lends unearned rigor.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the modifier: "two online experiments (n=247 and n=248)"."

**Issue B. Rating source specified beyond abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Advice centrality then mediated effects on leadership emergence and supervisor performance ratings"
- **Abstract says:** "Advice network centrality further mediates the interactive effects of gender and prosocial motivation on leadership emergence and performance ratings."
- **Problem:** The abstract says only "performance ratings" and does not identify the rater; attributing them to supervisors is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "performance ratings" without naming the rating source."

**Issue C. Motivation vs. perception in headline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "but only if they're seen as highly prosocial"
- **Abstract says:** "women are less likely than men to occupy central positions in advice networks, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap"
- **Problem:** The construct is the woman's own prosocial motivation, not colleagues' perception of her as prosocial.
- **Suggested fix:** ""— but only if they are highly prosocially motivated"."

### Study 4: Status comes first: being liked and respected builds power faster than power builds respect
**Work ID:** W7214338919 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Competence added to mechanism** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "being seen as competent and communal does convert into real control"
- **Abstract says:** "status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status… perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry."
- **Problem:** The abstract identifies communality/communion as the explanatory perception; competence is not tested or named as the mechanism.
- **Suggested fix:** "Limit the claim to being seen as communal (warm, concerned for others)."

### Study 5: Moderately good-looking male founders fare best; for women, looks barely move the needle
**Work ID:** W7214669005 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: The UK's "bamboo ceiling" is real — but only for some Asian groups, and mostly for men
**Work ID:** W7220681324 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Direction of risk-tolerance mediator** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "partly explained by lower measured risk tolerance"
- **Abstract says:** "a pattern partly mediated by ethnic differences in risk tolerance"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports "ethnic differences" in risk tolerance without stating which group scored lower; the specific direction is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "partly mediated by ethnic differences in measured risk tolerance" or attribute the direction explicitly as an inference."

### Study 7: Founders with dark-triad traits pick co-founders very differently — and equity is their trigger
**Work ID:** W7220450586 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 8: Why bank AI projects stall: it's not the black box, it's the clash over what counts as proof
**Work ID:** W7221037317 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 9: The "identity pause": what perimenopausal workers did instead of pushing through
**Work ID:** W7220928682 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Career-stage claim not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Perimenopause affects most women, often at the peak career stage"
- **Abstract says:** "perimenopause, which is a naturally occurring physiological transition experienced by most women"
- **Problem:** "Most women" is supported; the "peak career stage" framing is an addition not present in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the career-stage clause or label it as context rather than a study finding."

**Issue B. Prescription outruns theory-building study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this suggests the useful organizational response is permission to ease off temporarily rather than accommodations aimed at restoring full performance of the old self"
- **Abstract says:** "our findings point to the criticality of an identity pause, which involves taking respite from striving to enact idealized identities… advancing research on the body–identity nexus, embodiment, and women and work."
- **Problem:** The abstract describes an individual-level embodiment mechanism; it does not compare organizational responses or test the effectiveness of any accommodation.
- **Suggested fix:** "Frame as a hypothesis the study raises for employers rather than what the evidence shows is "the useful organizational response"."

### Study 10: Side-hustle founders aren't on a runway to full-time — for many, hybrid is the destination
**Work ID:** W7214931138 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 11: When a supportive boss makes perfectionists work themselves into the ground
**Work ID:** W7219177765 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 12: For veterans going back to school, hope only pays off if it turns into action
**Work ID:** W7213930347 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Direct effects described as null** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Neither trait related to satisfaction on its own."
- **Abstract says:** "Structural equation modeling results suggested the relationship between hope agency thinking and satisfaction with life is indirect and operates through occupational engagement. Similarly, the relationship between proactive personality and satisfaction with life is also indirect and operates through occupational engagement."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that the relationships are indirect; it does not explicitly state that the direct associations were non-significant, so flatly asserting no standalone relationship goes slightly beyond the text.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "the link to life satisfaction ran through occupational engagement rather than directly"."

### Study 13: Harassed by a customer, with no one watching: what protects gig workers
**Work ID:** W7218644956 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mediator pathways conflated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "workers reported higher psychological distress and a greater sense of threat to the self, and in turn cut corners on the work itself (production deviance) and behaved more rudely or hostilely toward customers (interpersonal deviance)"
- **Abstract says:** "the indirect detrimental effects of CSH on production deviance and interpersonal deviance, through psychological distress and self-threat, respectively, were weaker for gig workers who had access to collective representation"
- **Problem:** The abstract pairs distress specifically with production deviance and self-threat specifically with interpersonal deviance; the digest presents both mediators as leading to both outcomes.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that distress fed production deviance while self-threat fed interpersonal deviance."

**Issue B. Unverified examples of collective representation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "workers who had access to some form of collective representation, such as a union, worker association or organized peer body"
- **Abstract says:** "gig workers who had access to collective representation than those who lacked such access"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not specify what forms of collective representation were measured; the illustrative list is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the examples or mark them as illustrative rather than as what was measured."

### Study 14: Money worries make employees angry — and the anger shows up in their work
**Work ID:** W7215113460 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal framing of time-lagged associations** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Money worries make employees angry — and the anger shows up in their work"
- **Abstract says:** "financial insecurity was indirectly associated with counterproductive work behaviour via anger … These findings identify anger as an affective pathway linking financial insecurity to detrimental work outcomes"
- **Problem:** The abstract consistently uses associational language for multi-wave correlational data; the headline and the body phrase "whether financial insecurity harms work behavior" assert causation. The caveats partly correct this.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "is linked to" / "goes with" in the headline and body."

**Issue B. Task-performance result generalized to both studies** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "In both, employees who felt their financial resources were inadequate or unstable reported more anger, and that anger predicted more counterproductive work behavior; evidence for an effect on task performance was weaker."
- **Abstract says:** "Study 1 … showed that financial insecurity was indirectly associated with counterproductive work behaviour via anger, with weaker evidence for task performance. Study 2 … replicated the indirect association between financial insecurity and counterproductive work behaviour through anger."
- **Problem:** The weaker task-performance evidence is reported only for Study 1; the abstract does not say task performance was examined in Study 2.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute the weaker task-performance finding to Study 1 specifically."

### Study 15: Why bold ideas die on the boss's desk: it depends on how creative the boss is
**Work ID:** W7214467692 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 16: Can you train people to make work more playful? Only if they do the exercises
**Work ID:** W7214211158 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 17: Not all career dithering is the same: five reasons people stall on big decisions
**Work ID:** W7214312495 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Strategic timing framed as adaptive** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "waiting for better information or working best near a deadline looks different from avoiding a decision to protect your ego."
- **Abstract says:** "Pressure thriving and strategic timing showed a more complex pattern: both were positively associated with the harnessing dimension of psychological flexibility, whereas strategic timing showed less consistently adaptive associations."
- **Problem:** The abstract explicitly notes strategic timing was less consistently adaptive; the "Why it matters" line presents it as a benign alternative to avoidance.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add that strategic timing showed less consistently adaptive associations, so it is not simply the "healthy" form of delay."

### Study 18: When the boss makes everything a moral issue, employees stop fixing problems
**Work ID:** W7220998881 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Added design detail for Study 1** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "an experience sampling study tracking employees and their supervisors over repeated daily measurements"
- **Abstract says:** "we conducted two complementary empirical studies: Study 1, an experience sampling investigation, and Study 2, a vignette‐based laboratory experiment."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no information about sampling frequency or whether supervisors as well as employees were surveyed; this is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Describe Study 1 simply as an experience sampling study without specifying daily measures or supervisor participation."

### Study 19: Office politics can fuel creativity — but only where the boss plays favorites on merit
**Work ID:** W7212394179 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderator stated as a necessary condition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Office politics can fuel creativity — but only where the boss plays favorites on merit"
- **Abstract says:** "performance-based LMX differentiation strengthened both the positive relationship between LMX and employee creativity and the conditional indirect effect of political skill on creativity through LMX"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports strengthening of an existing positive effect, not that the effect exists only under performance-based differentiation; "fuel" also asserts causation for cross-sectional survey data.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "Office politics is linked to creativity — and the link is strongest where the boss differentiates on merit"."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | A short nudge changed how managers responded to a downturn — and the effect grew over three months | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, N (414), five waves, blind supervisor-rated voice and the three-month growth all match. Two small wording slips: the abstract reports lower promotion focus (not a shift toward prevention focus) and says interventions "weakened" rather than broke the threat–voice association. |
| 2 | Overqualified and over 50: feeling underused pushes older workers to mentor, not to disengage | ✅ Accurate | Two three-wave field studies, N = 261 and N = 274 dyads, the generativity pathway and the mature-age HR practices moderator are all reported as in the abstract; caveats appropriately flag self-report, common method and the correlational design. |
| 3 | Women get asked for advice as often as men — but only if they're seen as highly prosocial | ⚠️ Minor issues | Samples (275; 247; 248) and the mediation model match. Small issues: the abstract does not describe the experiments as preregistered, does not specify who provided performance ratings, and measures prosocial motivation rather than how prosocial a woman is perceived to be. |
| 4 | Status comes first: being liked and respected builds power faster than power builds respect | ⚠️ Minor issues | Two project-team studies with bivariate dual change score models, three additional experiments, the communality mechanism and the formal/informal power robustness check are all reported faithfully. One story-angle addition ("competent") is not in the abstract. |
| 5 | Moderately good-looking male founders fare best; for women, looks barely move the needle | ✅ Accurate | Field study (359 founders), preregistered experiment (771 participants, AI-manipulated attractiveness), the inverted-U for men, the null for women and the non-replication of the gendered pattern alongside support for the two mediators are all accurately represented, and the caveats flag the failed replication. |
| 6 | The UK's "bamboo ceiling" is real — but only for some Asian groups, and mostly for men | ⚠️ Minor issues | FTSE 2011–2024 census, UK Biobank N=322,734, the Chinese/Indian contrast, the gender moderation and the robustness across survey and polygenic risk-tolerance measures all match.
